Chapter.Content: 24 — Waiting Times, Covariance, and Matrix Decomposition
Reading map · Previous chapter · Next chapter

The exponential distribution describes memoryless waiting times, while covariance captures how measurements vary together across dimensions. Matrix decompositions then reveal rotation-like structure, stretch, and numerical limitations in real data.
By the end: Derive waiting-time quantities and interpret covariance and matrix decompositions without confusing geometry with statistical variation.
Recall question: What does covariance’s off-diagonal structure say about two measured components, and when can a decomposition be non-unique?

6 Poisson counts in physical simulation
Poisson distributions can model idealized event arrivals, emission counts, radioactive decay counts, and photon detection under appropriate independence and rate assumptions.
But not every light-related or sensor-related count is Poisson.
Dead time, saturation, correlations, varying event rates, and detector processing can produce different distributions.
In rendering research, such distinctions matter when constructing physically motivated noise models or benchmarking stochastic estimators.

7 Numerical covariance repair
In practical code, a covariance estimate can contain a tiny negative eigenvalue due to floating-point error.
One simple repair for a symmetric matrix is to eigendecompose:
replace negative eigenvalues by zero:
then reconstruct:
For a real symmetric matrix, this is a nearest PSD projection in the Frobenius norm when no additional constraints are imposed.
But if the diagonal variances must remain fixed, or the result must be a correlation matrix with unit diagonal, simple eigenvalue clipping may not satisfy all requirements.
More sophisticated nearest-PSD or nearest-correlation methods may be necessary. Nicholas Higham’s work establishes important matrix-nearness formulations and algorithms for these problems.
Most importantly, a covariance repair modifies the model.

If a matrix has a significantly negative eigenvalue, do not simply clip it and claim everything is correct. First investigate whether the cause is numerical roundoff, incorrect covariance assembly, invalid parameterization, or an actual modeling mistake.

Singular directions explain reconstruction and variation

Use SVD to separate input directions, gains and output directions. Least squares, minimum norm, regularization, PCA and polar decomposition then become connected applications of maps already understood.
Why a matrix factorization is a change in how we see the map

A matrix is first a rule that transforms an input, not a rectangular block of numbers. If , then : the input passes through and then through . A factorization is useful when it exposes simpler actions whose composition equals the original one. This is the right starting point for singular value decomposition (SVD), because SVD is a coordinate choice that makes a complicated map look like independent one-dimensional channels.

Consider the two-coordinate map . It sends to . Each output depends on both input coordinates: the coordinates are coupled in this basis. A diagonal map such as instead sends to ; each coordinate evolves independently. Coupling is not always an intrinsic property of the physical transformation. It can be a consequence of how we chose coordinates.

For the symmetric example, the orthonormal directions and form the columns of . In the original basis, mixes and ; in the basis it has the diagonal representation . Coordinates and reveal the independent modes: is multiplied by three and is unchanged. The transformation itself did not change. We changed the frame in which we describe it.

An orthogonal matrix changes between orthonormal frames while preserving lengths and angles. In two dimensions a determinant- orthogonal matrix is a rotation; determinant also includes a reflection. “Rotate, scale, rotate” is an intuitive reading of SVD, but the precise description is “change to an orthonormal input basis, scale each coordinate independently, then express the result in an orthonormal output basis.” The input and output bases can differ because a rectangular map can take one space into another.

Eigenanalysis asks a square map to return a direction to itself up to scalar: . That is a useful but restrictive demand. SVD asks the more flexible question: can we choose an orthonormal input direction whose image is a scalar multiple of some orthonormal output direction ? The relation is , with . The input and output directions need not coincide. This distinction makes SVD available for every real rectangular matrix, even when eigenvectors are missing, complex, or numerically awkward.
Singular value decomposition covers every rectangular map

Eigenvectors are tied to square maps. A graphics transform may instead map an -dimensional input to an -dimensional measurement, and its input and output directions live in different spaces. singular value decomposition (SVD) handles that general case:

For real , and are orthogonal (or have orthonormal columns in a thin factorization), and is rectangular diagonal with nonnegative entries . In a complex problem transpose becomes conjugate transpose. The right singular vector is an input direction; sends it to the paired output direction. The singular value is the stretch. Unlike an eigenvector, this does not require input and output spaces to be the same.

The geometric story is “rotate or reflect the input coordinates, stretch along perpendicular axes, then rotate or reflect in the output space.” Orthogonal stages preserve length; the diagonal stage exposes the map’s true principal stretches. The singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of , but computing SVD by explicitly forming is often a poor numerical shortcut: it squares the condition number and may erase small singular information. Use this identity to understand, not automatically to implement.

Full SVD uses and . Thin/economy SVD keeps only the columns needed to represent , saving storage and work. If , compact rank-revealing forms retain nonzero singular directions. For rank-deficient matrices, zero singular values identify null directions. Singular vectors corresponding to repeated singular values are not individually unique: any orthonormal basis of the repeated subspace is valid. A sign flip of a paired pair also leaves the product unchanged.

For an arbitrary input , its coordinates in the right-singular-vector basis are . Then the map acts as , and the output in ordinary coordinates is . Thus

In singular coordinates each surviving channel follows : no input coefficient spills into a different output coefficient. The right singular vectors are in the domain ; the left singular vectors are in the codomain . This makes the two-basis structure explicit and avoids treating the factors as unexplained symbols.

The unit sphere in input space remains a sphere through the orthogonal coordinate change . The diagonal stage turns it into an axis-aligned ellipsoid whose semiaxis lengths are the singular values. The final orthogonal change orients that ellipsoid in output space. Consequently for unit , the largest singular value is the largest possible 2-norm stretch, and is a direction that attains it:

A zero singular value collapses an input direction completely. A small positive singular value preserves that direction mathematically but nearly erases its magnitude, which makes reversal sensitive to noise. Singular values are nonnegative because a sign can be absorbed by changing the sign of a paired singular vector. A simultaneous sign flip of and leaves unchanged. When a singular value is repeated, its singular subspace is determined, while the particular orthonormal basis chosen inside that subspace is not unique.

When the exact rank is , the compact rank- SVD retains only the nonzero paired directions: , , and , with . A rectangular diagonal map also has a direct geometric reading. For example, maps to . It embeds a two-dimensional input into a plane in three-dimensional output space; the output cannot fill the third dimension. The two input singular directions receive independent stretches, and the unused output direction lies perpendicular to the range.
Rank, both nullspaces, and the four fundamental subspaces

If , exactly singular values are positive in exact arithmetic. The first right singular vectors span the row space, while the remaining right singular vectors span , since for each zero singular value. The first left singular vectors span . The remaining left singular vectors span because . Thus SVD places all four fundamental subspaces in paired orthogonal bases: row space with nullspace in the domain, column space with left nullspace in the codomain.

For the second column duplicates the first, so rank is one. Here has eigenvalues and , hence singular values and . The zero right singular vector points along , a change to the input that the matrix cannot observe. The surviving right vector points along and the surviving left vector spans the column direction . Rank deficiency is not an SVD failure: it is precisely the information SVD reveals.

Floating-point computations rarely produce a perfect zero for a theoretically rank-deficient matrix. A numerical rank rule may declare negligible when it is below a scale-relative cutoff, often related to , but the appropriate tolerance depends on measurement noise and application meaning. Multiplying all entries by a unit conversion factor should not arbitrarily change a relative rank decision. Conversely, a tiny singular value can encode a real but weakly measured direction rather than a dimension that is truly absent. Keep algebraic rank, numerical rank, and domain-specific confidence distinct.

Pseudoinverse makes least squares and minimum norm one operation

If is square and invertible, solves exactly. Real problems may be rectangular, inconsistent, or rank-deficient. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse generalizes inversion while respecting least squares and minimum norm. Its exact mathematical definition uses every strictly positive singular value:

In finite precision we often choose a threshold and reciprocate only singular values above it. Call that result , the truncated or numerical pseudoinverse. If a positive singular value is discarded, solves the retained-rank approximation of the problem; it need not minimize the original residual over every direction. The threshold is a policy tied to scale, precision, and application. Tiny singular values correspond to directions where inversion would magnify noise; discarding them states that those directions are not trusted at the selected resolution.

Take the rank-one matrix and target . Its SVD is already visible: and . The exact equation would require and , so no exact solution exists. Least squares sets and cannot change the second residual; every has residual . The minimum-norm member is , exactly what returns. This small example keeps three facts distinct: rank deficiency, inconsistency, and the extra minimum-norm rule.

Then is a least-squares minimizer of . If many minimizers have the same residual, it is the one with smallest Euclidean norm. For a consistent underdetermined system, that chooses the solution closest to zero. This is a principled choice, not proof that the minimum-norm answer is the only physically meaningful one; a graphics application may need regularization, constraints, or a prior.

The 2-norm condition number for a full-rank matrix is . For rank-deficient , it is infinite in the ordinary inverse sense. A large condition number means small data perturbations can cause large solution changes. Residual and solution error are different: a solver can produce a small residual while the solution remains highly sensitive. Report both when the distinction matters.

The truncated SVD also gives the best rank- approximation to in both spectral and Frobenius norms. Keeping the leading singular directions preserves the most energy under those measures; discarding the tail compresses information. Eckart–Young is the theorem that makes “keep the largest singular values” optimal for this specific approximation objective. It does not say the approximation is best for every perceptual, semantic, or downstream-engine objective.
The Moore–Penrose inverse and its four identities

For a full-column-rank square or rectangular matrix, inverse intuition still has limits: a rectangular matrix has no two-sided ordinary inverse, and a singular matrix cannot be inverted. SVD supplies the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Reverse the nonzero channels in reverse order: returns output coordinates to singular coordinates, reciprocates positive scales, and returns to the input basis:

The exact definition uses every strictly positive singular value, however small. In a full factorization the pseudoinverse has shape . For invertible square , it equals . Zero singular directions are assigned zero in ; division by zero is never attempted.
The four Moore–Penrose identities are

The first two express inverse-like consistency on the portions of the map that can be reached and recovered. The symmetry conditions make and orthogonal projections rather than oblique projections. Specifically, projects output vectors onto ; projects input vectors onto . For the SVD, these are and respectively. These projection meanings are more useful than memorizing the identities without context.

A small positive singular value makes its reciprocal large. If , exact multiplies the corresponding output coefficient by . That is mathematically correct for the exact map but can magnify measurement noise catastrophically. This is why the distinction between exact pseudoinverse and truncated pseudoinverse matters. Given a threshold , define by reciprocating only singular values satisfying and setting the rest to zero. This is a rank decision and a modeling policy. If it discards any positive singular values, does not in general minimize the residual over all for the original matrix: it solves using the retained singular subspace and may leave a residual component that an omitted positive direction could have reduced. Exact , by contrast, uses all positive directions and produces an original-problem least-squares minimizer. Thresholding may be more useful in noisy settings, but it trades residual fit for stability and must be named accurately.
Least squares from decoupling, then minimum norm
Consider . Insert the SVD and use orthogonality, which preserves the Euclidean norm. Let and . Then

The least-squares problem has become independent scalar problems, one per singular direction. For every positive singular value, choose , which matches that output coordinate. A zero singular direction cannot affect the output, so its coefficient does not change residual size. Among all minimizers, setting each such free coefficient to zero gives the smallest input norm because is orthogonal and . Therefore , . This proves both claims: exact pseudoinverse solution minimizes the original Euclidean residual, then chooses the minimum-norm solution among residual minimizers.

The same logic also explains the projection residual. The component of in is matched; the orthogonal component is unreachable and remains as residual. In exact arithmetic, the least-squares residual obeys , so it is perpendicular to every column of . This geometry is the least-squares normal condition, derived without needing to solve normal equations.

For an inconsistent rank-deficient example, let and . The second output coordinate cannot be produced, so no exact solution exists. Any gives the same residual ; the pseudoinverse selects because a nullspace component only increases norm. For an underdetermined consistent example, let and . Every solution satisfies . Write . Its squared norm is , minimized at . Thus , the shortest solution. These are distinct decisions: least squares minimizes residual first; minimum norm breaks ties between residual minimizers.

A minimum-norm answer is a mathematical convention based on the Euclidean metric, not automatic proof of physical appropriateness. If variables have different units, costs, or prior plausibility, rescaling, constraints, or regularization may be needed. The pseudoinverse gives a precise baseline whose assumptions can be inspected.
Conditioning: weak singular directions amplify uncertainty
For invertible square , the largest stretch is and the largest stretch of is . Therefore

A rank-deficient matrix has zero smallest singular value and infinite ordinary condition number. The same ratio of largest to smallest positive singular value describes the conditioning on the nonzero subspace for full-rank rectangular problems. Geometrically this is the long-axis to short-axis ratio of the ellipsoid: a nearly spherical image is well-conditioned, a very thin pancake is sensitive, and a flattened dimension is noninvertible.

A large condition number says that small perturbations in data can create large changes in a recovered solution. It does not say every particular residual is large. A solve can fit the supplied measurements with a tiny residual while its coefficients remain highly sensitive to a small measurement perturbation. Residual error and solution sensitivity are different quantities. Condition numbers also depend on units and parameterization: scaling one input variable changes the numerical singular spectrum, so sensible nondimensionalization may be important.

Because the eigenvalues of are squared singular values, its condition number is the square of ’s. This is another way to understand why the Gram-matrix route is risky in floating-point arithmetic. The identity is explanatory; robust numerical routines should avoid constructing the Gram matrix as a shortcut when small singular values matter.
Low-rank approximation and why the largest directions win
Expanding the factorization by columns gives

Each summand is rank one. Acting on , it first measures the component , scales it by , and emits it along . A matrix is therefore a sum of independent rank-one input-output channels. Keeping the first terms creates , with rank at most . This is useful for compression when is much smaller than both dimensions: dense storage costs values, while the factors cost approximately values.
The Eckart–Young result says that this truncation is not merely plausible: it is a best rank- approximation under two important norms. In spectral norm,
and in Frobenius norm,

The spectral error is the strongest discarded channel; the Frobenius error combines squared energy across all discarded channels. Here is the dimension argument for the spectral lower bound. For and any with , its null space has dimension at least . If , the truncated approximation is exact and both lower bounds are zero. The span has dimension , so contains a nonzero vector. Normalize one to . Then , while implies ; hence . Truncation attains this bound.

For the Frobenius lower bound, choose an orthonormal matrix whose columns lie in . Then . Multiplication by an orthonormal-column matrix cannot increase Frobenius norm, so . In right-singular coordinates, this trace is , where is the squared length of row of . Because has orthonormal columns, and . The smallest weighted sum assigns weight one to the smallest values of and zero to the others, giving at least (pad with zeros when ). The truncated SVD attains this Frobenius bound too.

The guarantee is tied to the chosen matrix norm and low-rank objective. It does not promise best perceptual quality, best downstream rendering, or best prediction accuracy. A domain-specific weighting can change which directions matter. Frobenius energy retained after components is , a common summary for PCA or compression, but that ratio is not a universal quality score.
Thresholding and regularization are different choices

A rank-based truncation keeps exactly leading singular values. An absolute cutoff retains values above ; a relative cutoff can retain values satisfying . These choices answer different questions. A fixed rank can meet a storage budget. A scale-relative threshold can mark directions too weak relative to the dominant one. A noise model may imply a different cutoff. Numerical rank is never solely a property of a floating-point array without a precision and tolerance policy.

Truncated SVD pseudoinversion sets weak reciprocals to zero. This removes unstable directions completely: it reduces noise amplification but introduces bias and may increase the original residual because omitted positive directions are no longer used. Smooth regularization uses a different filter. For example, Tikhonov/ridge regularization solves a penalized problem . In singular coordinates its coefficient filter is applied to , rather than either or a hard zero/reciprocal switch. Small directions are damped continuously instead of abruptly discarded. Both methods express a preference for stability over exact inversion of weakly observed information, but they encode different assumptions and objectives.

For SVD compression, truncating small values approximates the matrix itself. For solving inverse problems, truncating singular values modifies how measurements map back to parameters. Those operations share a spectrum but are not the same task. State whether the goal is best rank- approximation, a numerical-rank solve, or a regularized inverse before interpreting a cutoff.
SVD in a graphics sensitivity picture

A local graphics transform or Jacobian maps small perturbations to . SVD tells which input perturbations are amplified, which are suppressed, and in which output directions the effect appears. A small input sphere becomes an ellipsoid. The axes are sensitive input directions, are gains, and axes show the response directions. This interpretation applies to deformation gradients, inverse problems, camera sensitivity, mesh processing, optimization Jacobians, covariance analysis, and shape variation.

The singular basis also explains why SVD connects so many topics. Rank counts surviving channels. Nullity counts erased input channels. The row and column spaces are the input and output spans of surviving directions. Pseudoinversion reverses surviving channels. Least squares projects onto reachable outputs. Minimum norm removes arbitrary nullspace components. Conditioning compares the strongest and weakest channels. Low-rank approximation discards selected channels under a stated error measure. Each concept is a different question about the same geometry, so the equations, data, and implementation can be checked against one another.
Why the pseudoinverse identities follow from projections
The four Moore–Penrose relations become almost mechanical in compact SVD coordinates. Let with all entries of the square positive, and let . Then

These are symmetric idempotent matrices because and . They project onto the column and row spaces. Applying to keeps every column-space component, so . Applying to keeps every row-space component, so . Symmetry gives the remaining two identities. This derivation shows what the properties guarantee: the operator behaves like an inverse on the rank- subspaces and like zero on orthogonal complements. For a full-column-rank tall matrix, ; for a full-row-rank wide matrix, . In the opposite products, the identity is only a projection unless the map is square and invertible.

This is also a useful dimensional check. With , its pseudoinverse is , so is and acts on outputs, while is and acts on inputs. Accidentally reversing and can produce products with plausible square shapes while projecting onto the wrong space; naming each factor’s domain and codomain catches that error.

Chapter.Content: PCA turns a cloud of points into measured variation

Principal component analysis begins with data, not with a mysterious covariance matrix. Put samples in the rows of a data table . Compute each feature mean and subtract it from every sample. Without centering, the dominant direction may point toward the cloud’s offset from the origin instead of along the cloud’s variation.
For centered , sample covariance is

The divisor may be in a population convention; state which convention you use. For a unit direction , the projected scores are and their sample variance is . Maximizing this quadratic form under gives an eigenvector of for the largest eigenvalue. Requiring the next component to be orthogonal gives the next eigenvector. Eigenvalues are variances along those principal directions.

There is a direct SVD route. If , the columns of are principal directions and the scores are . Covariance eigenvalues are . This avoids explicitly forming , which can improve numerical behavior for data with a wide range of scales. PCA is not automatically scale invariant: changing units of one feature changes its variance and therefore its influence. Standardization is a separate modeling decision that changes the question.

For graphics, PCA can estimate a point-cloud plane: the eigenvector for the smallest covariance eigenvalue is a candidate normal, while the other two span the best-fit plane. If the cloud is nearly a line, two small eigenvalues make the plane normal ambiguous. If the eigenvalues are close, small perturbations can rotate individual principal axes substantially even while the subspace remains stable. A useful application should reason about the eigengap and the subspace, not just print three axes.

For a minimal worked cloud, take centered samples , , . With divisor , the covariance is . The first principal direction is horizontal and carries variance one; the perpendicular direction carries zero variance. If small vertical noise is added, the second eigenvalue becomes small rather than exactly zero. Whether it is treated as signal or discarded is a modeling decision supported by noise scale, not an algebraic truth hidden in the word “PCA.”
Centered measurements reveal principal directions

Principal component analysis (PCA) asks a geometric question about a cloud of samples: along which directions does it vary most, second most, and so on? Let there be samples with measured features. Use the row-sample convention , so row is . Samples must be finite. The sample-covariance path requires : reject empty input because the mean is undefined and reject a singleton as insufficient for an unbiased sample covariance. An API may instead explicitly choose population covariance with divisor ; that permits and returns zero covariance, but still must define empty-input behavior. The mean is . Center each sample, , and place those rows in . Centering ensures . This removes translation: a cloud shifted far from the origin has the same shape and variation after centering. Without centering, the offset itself can dominate squared coordinates, causing the first component to describe location instead of spread.

A direction must be normalized before comparing its variance with another direction. For unit , the scalar coordinate of centered sample along that direction is . Its sample variance, using the sample convention , is

Chapter.Content: The bracketed matrix is the covariance . Thus variance in unit direction is the Rayleigh quotient . Maximizing this subject to gives an eigenvector of for its largest eigenvalue: use a Lagrange multiplier on to obtain . The largest eigenvalue is the greatest attainable variance. The second component maximizes variance subject to perpendicularity to the first; continuing gives orthonormal eigenvectors of the symmetric covariance. Eigenvalues are variances along those axes.

For a direct computation, consider the centered 2D samples , , , and . Their sample mean is zero. Summing outer products gives , so with divisor , . Every direction has the same variance and no unique principal axis exists: the two eigenvalues are repeated. If the second coordinates are instead , the sum of outer products is and covariance is . The horizontal axis carries four times the variance of the vertical. These calculations make the meaning of the eigenvalues concrete and show why equal or close eigenvalues make individual axes ambiguous.

The covariance entry measures co-variation between features and . Diagonal entries are individual feature variances; positive off-diagonal entries mean deviations tend to have the same sign, while negative values mean opposite signs. These terms are coordinate coupling. If and transformed sample coordinates are , then their covariance is . The eigenbasis removes cross-covariance because all off-diagonal coupling vanishes in those coordinates. Covariance is positive semidefinite: for any , . A zero eigenvalue therefore means there is no measured variation along its eigenvector. If points lie in a plane in 3D, the normal direction has zero variance; the two large-eigenvalue directions span the best-fit plane. With noise, the smallest-eigenvalue eigenvector remains the least-variance normal estimate, and its reliability depends on the gap between that small eigenvalue and the next one.
PCA can instead use a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centered data, . Substitute this into covariance:

Because , the right singular vectors (columns of ) are covariance eigenvectors, and covariance eigenvalues are . Keeping the first directions in , the principal scores are . An approximate reconstruction is , where the mean is added back to every row. By the Eckart–Young theorem this is the best rank- approximation in Frobenius norm. A point-cloud plane fit is the same recipe: subtract the centroid, form a 3-by-3 covariance or use data SVD, then take the eigenvector of that covariance, equivalently the right singular vector of the centered sample matrix, associated with its smallest eigenvalue/singular value as the normal. Left singular vectors live in sample space , so they are not the 3D feature-space normal. A thin, noisy, or nearly collinear cloud may not determine a stable plane; the eigengap and noise level matter.

Feature units alter the result. If one coordinate is in millimeters and another in meters, a numerical rescaling changes covariance and therefore PCA. Standardizing each feature by a scale produces correlation-based PCA and asks a different question: relative variation after unit normalization instead of absolute physical variance. Neither convention is automatically correct. Record whether the data was centered only, centered and standardized, or weighted, since the output axes depend on that modeling decision.
Plane fits, eigengaps, and interpretation of uncertain components

For centered 3D points , a plane through the centroid with unit normal has signed residual distance . The sum of squared distances is . Minimizing it under selects the eigenvector for the smallest covariance eigenvalue. This is the same direction that PCA describes as having the least variance. The two other eigenvectors span the fitted plane. For example, a flat tabletop cloud might have covariance eigenvalues : the last direction is a clear normal candidate. If instead they are , the two low directions are close, and the estimated normal is sensitive to small noise; there is no strong evidence separating one normal from another within that plane-like subspace. Eigenvalue magnitudes tell variance, while the gap measures axis identifiability. Reporting a normal without examining this gap can give false confidence.

The sample divisor is a convention with consequences. The unbiased sample covariance estimator uses when the mean is estimated from the same samples; population covariance uses . This changes eigenvalues and score variance by a scalar factor but does not change eigenvectors when all features share the same divisor. Weights also change the geometric question: a weighted covariance gives more influence to selected observations. For large data, a streaming mean and covariance algorithm can avoid storing every sample, but the same centered-data interpretation still applies. If the stored matrix is rows=features rather than rows=samples, transpose formulas accordingly; writing the shape next to each product prevents accidental computation of when the intended feature covariance is .
Polar decomposition separates rotation-like motion from stretch
SVD also gives the polar decomposition of a real square matrix:

where is positive semidefinite and is orthogonal when is nonsingular. For singular , an orthogonal completion may not be unique. This is the right polar form: first apply stretch , then orthogonal motion under column-vector composition. A left polar form uses .

The symmetric stretch can include shear in the original basis; “symmetric” does not mean “diagonal scale in the current coordinates.” If , the orthogonal factor may include a reflection. It is therefore not always a pure rotation in . This distinction matters in graphics where a mirrored transform changes handedness and normal orientation.

In an SVD, and for the nonsingular case. This makes polar decomposition a concise way to ask: what orthogonal part and what symmetric stretch combine to produce this deformation? For a deformation gradient, it separates the local rigid-like motion from strain-like change, though the exact interpretation depends on the physical model and frame.
Polar decomposition separates frame dependent stretch from orientation

The polar decomposition separates a linear map into an orthogonal factor and a symmetric positive-semidefinite stretch. For square , the right polar form is , where is orthogonal and is the right stretch. For rectangular maps the analogous orthogonal factor is a partial isometry, not a square orthogonal matrix; the square case is the one used for rotation extraction below. If is square and invertible, derive by multiplying the equation by its transpose: , since and . The positive-semidefinite square root is therefore , and then . The symmetric stretch has orthonormal principal axes: in its eigenbasis it scales each axis by a nonnegative amount, without a net rotation. The orthogonal factor carries the remaining orientation, including a possible reflection.

There is also a left polar form with . The right stretch is measured in the input or material frame; the left stretch is measured in the output or spatial frame. They are generally different matrices because the frames differ. For a concrete check, let and let be a 30-degree rotation. Then : the first coordinate is stretched by 2 and the second by one half in the principal frame, then the result is rotated. A shear can also have a nonidentity polar orthogonal factor: although the matrix is described as a shear, it changes the orientation of vectors, and polar decomposition assigns part of that change to the best orthogonal component. In deformation gradients, this split lets a model remove rigid rotation before measuring elastic strain.

From SVD, , regroup factors as . Hence and . The first is orthogonal; the second is symmetric PSD. Also , so its positive square root is exactly . The analogous left stretch is , yielding . For nonsingular square , the right polar orthogonal factor is unique. In singular directions, collapses vectors to zero, so its action cannot determine how an orthogonal factor should map those unobserved directions; completions can differ while the product remains valid.

An orthogonal matrix has determinant either or . Only determinant belongs to , the group of proper rotations. If has determinant , it includes a reflection. Applications that require a proper rotation, such as rigid pose alignment, need an explicit nearest- rule, commonly a sign correction on a singular direction with smallest singular value; this changes the optimality problem to constrain orientation and must be stated. In this determinant-correction case, if the least singular value is repeated, multiple choices tie and the nearest proper rotation is nonunique; a zero least singular value also permits freedom in its null direction. Repeated singular values alone do not make the nearest proper rotation nonunique when no determinant correction is needed. Never label every orthogonal factor “rotation” without checking determinant.
Two-sided rotations, nearest proper rotation, and nonunique directions

Two-sided Jacobi can be understood by looking at a local block . First choose a right rotation that diagonalizes ; this makes the two columns of orthogonal. Then choose a left rotation that aligns those perpendicular columns with coordinate axes, equivalently diagonalizing . The updated local block is diagonal up to signs. Embedded in the full identity, these rotations act on selected column and row pairs. The right transformations accumulate into and the left transformations into . A sweep repeats across pairs. This local 2-by-2 SVD view explains both sides of the algorithm: right rotations remove input-direction coupling; left rotations align the corresponding output directions. Unlike one-sided Jacobi, the working matrix itself is driven toward diagonal form rather than merely toward mutually orthogonal columns.

For a square nonsingular matrix, the orthogonal polar factor is the closest orthogonal matrix to in Frobenius norm. To see why, for any orthogonal , expand . The first two terms do not depend on , so minimizing distance maximizes . Substitute and let , also orthogonal. Then the trace is , because each diagonal entry of an orthogonal matrix is at most one. Equality is attained by , giving .

If the requirement is a proper rotation with determinant , then when one must force . The best trace is then obtained by assigning the required sign reversal to a direction with smallest singular value. With singular values in descending order, let ; the constrained minimizer is . Its stretch/error cost reflects the smallest direction. In this determinant-correction case, a repeated least singular value gives tied sign-reversal directions and a nonunique nearest proper rotation; a zero least singular value permits freedom in its null direction. Repeated singular values alone do not imply nonuniqueness when already has determinant . This is a constrained Procrustes choice, not the same unconstrained polar orthogonal factor when that factor reflects.
How numerical software computes and checks an SVD

Reliable SVD algorithms do not usually diagonalize directly. A common route first uses Householder transformations to reduce a dense matrix to bidiagonal form: nonzeros remain only on the main diagonal and one neighboring diagonal. These orthogonal transformations preserve singular values while concentrating the work into a simpler structure. Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization names this reduction process; it should not be confused with every later iterative bidiagonal solver.

Jacobi SVD methods repeatedly rotate column pairs toward orthogonality. In one-sided Jacobi, the working matrix columns are orthogonalized directly and their norms become singular values; the accumulated rotations build right singular vectors. This can provide excellent relative accuracy for small singular values, but sweep counts and stopping tests must be explicit. A maximum sweep count is essential: failure to converge is an outcome to return, not a loop to hide.

After computation, sort singular values in descending order and permute corresponding columns of and together. Choose a sign convention only for presentation consistency; no sign convention removes the nonuniqueness of repeated singular subspaces. Temporal applications may need to align signs or subspaces between frames to avoid visually jumping axes.
Validation checks reconstruction and orthogonality. For a computed , use a scaled residual such as

and check and with dimensions appropriate to full or thin output. A zero input needs a defined denominator policy. Checking only column lengths is insufficient: columns can each have unit length and still fail to be mutually perpendicular. Reconstruction alone is also insufficient if factors are nonorthogonal but happen to multiply to a close matrix. Both classes of invariant matter.
